Thanks again for the time today. Quick recap + next steps from our call with the engineering team so we can align on performance SLOs and concurrency requirements before the technical deep-dive.

High-level ask from Acme:
- Latency SLO: p95 <= 200ms for text-generation endpoints (single-turn inference).
- Streaming: required for token-by-token updates to user UI (websocket or chunked HTTP streaming).
- Throughput: expected steady state ~150 requests/sec with peak bursts to ~2,000 requests/sec during promotions.
- Concurrency: estimated 400–600 concurrent streams/long-lived connections.
- Token profile: average request ~150 tokens in, ~300 tokens generated.

From Redwood: we need to confirm a few items to size Dedicated and rate-limits properly:
1) Typical request shape: will bursts be short (seconds) vs. sustained (minutes)?
2) Are streams long-lived (minutes) or short-lived (seconds)?
3) Do you need guaranteed per-route concurrency (e.g., dedicated pool for Payments UI) or is multi-tenant shared acceptable?

Immediate next steps I propose:
- Acme to confirm burst duration and expected daily request volume.
- Schedule a 60–90 minute technical deep-dive with Dev to test streaming and measure end-to-end latency on a sample workload.
- I attached a mutual_action_plan.pdf and our redwood-dedicated-quotas.xlsx to illustrate Dedicated sizing options and typical rate-limit profiles.

If you can reply with the answers to 1–3 above, we’ll draft a proposed Dedicated configuration and a rate-limit proposal (including burst windows and fallback policies).

Thanks —

Marissa — thanks for the clear recap. A few clarifications from our side:

- Burst profile: most bursts are short (30–90 seconds) but can repeat often during promotional events; we also have a few expected windows of sustained traffic (5–20 minutes) during nightly settlement windows.
- Stream length: typical user-facing streams are short (10–30s) for chat use; however, some backend reconciliation jobs may open longer streams (several minutes).
- We would prefer guaranteed per-route concurrency for the Payments UI, since latency there directly affects checkout conversion. Shared pools are acceptable for lower-priority workloads.

Numbers we should plan for:

- Peak burst target: 2,000 rps for 1–2 minutes during flash events.
- Sustained peak: 150–250 rps for short windows.
- Concurrent long-lived connections: target 500 concurrent streams for Payments UI (with graceful degradation).

On rate limits: what does Redwood recommend for connection pooling and 429 behavior? We need to know how you handle burst smoothing, token buckets, and whether you support per-route burst overrides if we commit to reserved capacity.

Happy to get the technical deep-dive on the calendar — Sophie and I are available Thu/Fri next week.

John/Sophie — quick technical notes ahead of the deep-dive. Happy to walk through these in the meeting.

Streaming & connections:
- Redwood supports both chunked HTTP streaming and WebSocket-based streaming. For browser UIs we typically recommend chunked HTTP or HTTP/2 streams; for mobile with unstable networks, websocket with reconnect logic is fine.
- Long-lived streams (minutes) should be treated differently: they consume a concurrent slot on the serving pool for the duration of the stream.

Concurrency & pooling:
- Concurrency is expressed as number of concurrent inference sessions (long-lived streams) + short RPCs. We size Dedicated pools by concurrent slots and per-slot throughput.
- For your profile (avg tokens noted by Marissa), a conservative sizing estimate: ~1 Dedicated GPU worker can sustain 100–150 short requests/sec (non-streaming) or ~40–60 concurrent token-streams depending on model and sequence length.
- Connection pooling best practices: use a small pool of persistent connections per app process (5–20 connections) and multiplex multiple logical sessions over those where possible. This reduces TCP/TLS churn and is more predictable with Redwood’s token-based cost controls.

Rate limits & quotas:
- Redwood enforces per-account and per-route quotas with configurable token-bucket parameters. Default hosted limits are modest; Dedicated customers can negotiate higher steady-state and burst windows.
- Typical pattern we recommend for Acme: reserve a Dedicated pool sized for sustained concurrency (500 slots) and a burst window for shared hosted capacity up to 2,000 rps for short bursts (30–120s).
- 429 policy: client gets 429 when bucket is exhausted; we provide Retry-After and a recommended exponential backoff. For critical routes, we can configure graceful fallbacks (lower-quality model variant) instead of immediate 429s.

What we need from you before sizing:
- A simple request distribution sample (CSV or traces) showing timestamp, tokens_in, tokens_out for 1–2 representative days.
- Confirmation if Payments UI needs hard isolation (no noisy neighbors) vs. soft isolation.

I’ve attached a short PDF with sample rate-limit configs (sample-rate-limits.pdf). If you can share a trace export, I’ll run a quick capacity estimate and bring numbers to the deep-dive.

Thanks —
